SEC26A-01.explanation: The subject is "the young," an adjective used as a noun to mean young birds, and such a noun is always plural, so the verb must be "are answering." The begging belongs to "the nestlings" named in the opening phrase, which is also plural, so the possessive must be "their." "Is answering their" gets the possessive right but treats "the young" as a singular group, the way "the brood" would be. "Are answering its" has the right verb but gives the begging a singular owner, and the only singular candidate, "the breeding female," is the bird that cannot keep up, not the one begging. "Is answering its" makes both errors, reading "the young" as a single unit throughout.

SEC26A-02.explanation: The subject is the distributive pronoun "Each," which is singular by rule; "patients" and "wards" sit inside the phrases that follow it. The tense is fixed by "when the sponsor put the trial on hold": "put" has the same form in the present and the past, but with the singular "the sponsor" the present would be "puts," so "put" is past and the diary keeping happened at a past moment, which requires "was keeping." "Is keeping" has the right number, and the present-tense description of the trial and the present "keep" later in the sentence make it look right, but it cannot be paired with a past when-clause. "Were keeping" has the right tense but takes its number from the plural nouns, and "are keeping" makes both errors.

SEC26A-03.explanation: The first sentence says the bank sorts its seed by hillside and gives each hillside a tray, so the freezer holds several trays, and "the tray" alone does not say which one failed. The phrase "kept nearest the freezer's door" is what identifies it, so it is restrictive and takes no punctuation. "Tray, kept" and "tray—kept" set the phrase off as extra information, which would imply the freezer holds only one tray. "Tray kept," treats "kept" as complete on its own and leaves "nearest the freezer's door" stranded with nothing to modify, separating the participle from the phrase that completes it.

SEC26A-04.explanation: The subject is the singular "ointment"; "clinics," the plural noun that opens the sentence, sits in an introductory phrase and does not govern the verb. The clause "since the network's doctors voted last spring" measures a span running from a past event up to the present, and a main clause tied to such a since-clause must be in the present perfect, so "has been prescribed" is correct. "Was prescribed" has the right number and matches the definite past "last spring" and the past "did not rise" in the next sentence, but the simple past cannot be paired with a since-clause of this kind; "last spring" dates the vote, not the prescribing. "Have been prescribed" has the right aspect but takes its number from "clinics," and "were prescribed" makes both errors.

SEC26A-05.explanation: The subject is the plural "needles"; "pine," the singular noun right before the blank, is the object of "beneath," so the verb must be "are decomposed." The agent is "bacteria," named in the clause "where surveys detect acid-tolerant bacteria"; "bacteria" is the plural of "bacterium," so the pronoun must be "them." "Are decomposed by it" has the right verb but treats "bacteria" as a singular mass, a common error. "Is decomposed by them" has the right agent but takes its number from "pine," and "is decomposed by it" makes both errors.

SEC26A-06.explanation: The subject is "oats," a plural noun, even though grain is often spoken of as a mass; "farm," the singular noun of the opening phrase, does not govern the verb. The auxiliary is decided nine words later by "rotten," which is an adjective, not a past participle (the participle of "rot" is "rotted"), so it needs a form of "be": "were seldom ... rotten." "Have seldom" has the right number, and "rotten" looks like a participle such as "gotten," but "have seldom rotten" lacks "been." "Was seldom" uses "be" but treats the oats as a singular mass or takes its number from "farm," and "has seldom" makes both errors.

SEC26A-07.explanation: The words after the blank read at first like an appositive defining catgut ("the tough cord twisted from the dried intestines of sheep and goats"), but the verb "had" arrives twelve words later, so they are the subject of a new independent clause. That clause already uses a colon of its own ("market: the string makers"), and a sentence cannot carry two colons in sequence, so the clauses must be separated by a period. "Catgut, the" joins two independent clauses with only a comma, a comma splice. "Catgut the" runs them together with no punctuation. "Catgut: the" would put a second colon into a sentence whose later colon introduces the string makers, and in any case the cord's market among string makers does not explain how surgeons closed wounds.

SEC26A-08.explanation: The subject is "pancreas," a singular noun that happens to end in -s (its plural is "pancreases"); "mice," the plural noun right before the blank, is the object of "of." The tense is set by the conditional "unless the animals receive a drug," whose present-tense verb states a general outcome and requires a present-tense main clause, so "is damaged" is correct. "Are damaged" has the right tense but treats the subject as plural. "Was damaged" has the right number but shifts to the past, which the report of the experiments in the last sentence invites and the present "receive" rules out. "Were damaged" makes both errors.

SEC26A-09.explanation: The harvest that fell is the cooperative's, and the first sentence shows that the cooperative is the founder plus the neighbors she persuaded to sell their fruit under its label, so it belongs to several growers and the noun must be the plural possessive "growers'." "Grower's" points to one grower, and the only single grower in the passage, the founder, is ruled out by the end of the sentence: her own trees lost almost nothing. "Growers" without an apostrophe invites reading "harvest" as a verb ("the growers harvest"), but the sentence's verb is "fell," so "harvest" is a noun and needs a possessive before it. "Grower" is neither plural nor possessive.

SEC26A-10.explanation: "The vines" looks at first like the object of "spray," but the main verb "were showing" arrives six words later and needs a subject, and "the vines growing along the lowest terraces" is that subject. "Spray" is used here without an object, so the introductory clause ends after "spray," and the comma goes there. "Spray the vines," treats "the vines" as the object and leaves "were showing" with no subject. "Spray the vines" with no comma has the same problem and runs the clause into the sentence. "Spray; the vines" uses a semicolon after a dependent clause beginning with "Before," which cannot stand as an independent clause.

SEC26B-01.explanation: The verb's subject is the plural "engineers" ("the radio engineers at both tracking stations"), not the singular "probe's" or "report" in the opening clause, so the verb is "have reconstructed." What the engineers reconstructed is the opening clause's "last status report," named almost thirty words before the blank and singular, so the pronoun is "it"; "burst" renames that same report. "Have reconstructed them" carries the verb's plural number onto the pronoun, but the plural nouns near the blank, "engineers" and "stations," are the reconstructors and their workplaces, not the thing rebuilt. "Has reconstructed it" and "has reconstructed them" pair a singular verb with the plural "engineers."

SEC26B-02.explanation: The subject is the singular "front" ("the glacier's calving front"); "currents" and "crevasses" belong to the opening participial phrase, so the verb is singular. The tense is set by the habitual clause "whenever the meltwater lakes that pool on the upper ice in midsummer drain through cracks to the bed": its verbs "pool" and "drain" are present (the past would be "pooled" and "drained"), and a present habitual clause requires a present main verb, so "is prone" is correct. "Was prone" follows the past narration around it ("photographed," "captured"), but a past main verb cannot govern a present "whenever" clause. "Are prone" and "were prone" are plural, agreeing with "crevasses" or "lakes" rather than with "front," and "were prone" also clashes with the present clause.

SEC26B-03.explanation: The words after the blank form a complete clause: its subject is "the fainter mark along the lowest weld of the main girder," and its verb, "tore," arrives eleven words after the blank, so two independent clauses meet at the blank. With no conjunction, they are joined by a semicolon. A comma reads "the fainter mark ..." as an appositive renaming "line" until "tore" arrives, and then leaves a comma splice. A colon is ruled out because the sentence already uses its colon after "abutment" to introduce the two defects, and a sentence takes only one colon; no mark at all fuses the two clauses.

SEC26B-04.explanation: The subject is the plural "segments"; "dome" belongs to the opening phrase and "mirror's" only modifies the head, so the verb is plural. The phrase "on the evening of the observatory's yearly open house" pins the cleaning to one particular occasion, and a specific point in time takes the simple past, not the present perfect, so "were cleaned" is correct. "Have been cleaned" is plural and tempts because the cleaned mirror "gathers" more light now, but the present perfect cannot be tied to a named occasion such as "the evening of the ... open house." "Has been cleaned" makes the same error with a singular verb, and "was cleaned" is singular, agreeing with "dome" or "mirror's" rather than with "segments."

SEC26B-05.explanation: The blank stands in for a verb that the main clause supplies later: the steel tapes lengthen, so the elided verb is the present lexical verb of "barely lengthens in summer heat," and an elided present lexical verb is represented by a form of "do." The subject of the opening clause is the plural "tapes," so "do" rather than "does." "Does" tempts because the main clause's subject, "a tape of invar," is singular and its verb is "lengthens," but that noun belongs to a different clause. "Was" and "were" are forms of "be," which cannot stand in for "lengthens"; the historical setting of "nineteenth-century survey crews" makes them attractive, but the main clause offers no form of "be" for them to echo.

SEC26B-06.explanation: The verb's subject is the singular "receiver"; "domes" is part of the phrase "beside the observatory's twin domes," so the verb is "is tracking." What the receiver tracks is named at the start of the sentence, "grains this small," a plural noun more than twenty words before the blank, so the pronoun is "them" even though the verb is singular. "Is tracking it" copies the subject's singular number onto the pronoun, but the receiver cannot be the object of its own verb and no singular noun in the sentence is being tracked. "Are tracking them" and "are tracking it" make the verb plural, agreeing with "domes" rather than with "receiver."

SEC26B-07.explanation: The introductory clause is "As the crew blasted the ridge": "the ridge" is the object of "blasted," and the main clause's own subject, "loosened boulders on the slopes above the valley road," follows, with its verb, "fell," ten words after the blank. A comma sets the introductory dependent clause off from the main clause, so it belongs after "ridge." A comma after "blasted" makes "the ridge loosened boulders on the slopes above the valley road" a complete main clause, which reads well until "fell" is left with no subject. With no comma, the same misreading ("the ridge loosened boulders") runs the clause's object into the main clause, and a semicolon cannot separate a dependent clause from the clause it introduces.

SEC26B-08.explanation: The subject is the plural "staves"; "wall" and "hearth" sit inside the phrase that locates them, so the verb is plural. The tense is set by the while-clause, whose own verb comes only at its end: "lining" is a participle, and the finite verb is "cooled," fifteen words after the blank, which places the work in the past and requires the past progressive "were being replaced." "Are being replaced" is plural but present; it tempts because the first sentence describes relining as a present process and "lining" reads as present, yet it cannot run alongside the past "cooled." "Was being replaced" is past but singular, agreeing with "hearth," and "is being replaced" is wrong in both number and tense.

SEC26B-09.explanation: The word before "sketches" must name their owner, and the first sentence implies there was exactly one: the hut had "a single bunk," and each page of its logbook "is signed in the same hand," so one observer lived there and made the sketches: "observer's." "Observers'" would credit several people; the plural "summer visitors" makes it tempting, but the visitors only found the sketches. "Observer" lets "sketches" read as a verb ("The observer sketches the hut's summer visitors"), a sentence that seems complete until "found" and "show" are left with no place in it. "Observers" is a plain plural that neither shows possession nor agrees with "sketches" read as a verb.

SEC26B-10.explanation: The blank separates the first two items in a series of three instruments. The third item, "a narrow-angle camera, the heaviest instrument aboard," contains its own commas, so every item in the series must be separated by a semicolon. A comma would be right only in a series whose items contain no commas, like "aluminum, titanium, and carbon fiber" earlier in the same sentence; here it would blur where one instrument ends and the next begins. A colon cannot divide two items within a list, and no mark runs "boom" into "a dust counter."

SEC26C-01.explanation: The subject of the verb is "the oldest drop curtain," a singular noun; the appositive "a harbor view rolled up in a loft above the stage" separates it from the verb, and "painters" and "backdrops" earlier in the sentence are not the subject. The curtain is contrasted, by "but," with the backdrops that "three hired scene painters restored," so the agent of the neglect is the plural "painters," and the pronoun must be "them." "Were neglected by them" and "were neglected by it" pair a plural verb with the singular "curtain." "Was neglected by it" has the right verb, but "it" could refer only to a singular noun such as "loft," "stage" or "auditorium," none of which can neglect anything, or to the curtain itself, which as subject would need a reflexive.

SEC26C-02.explanation: The subject "The illiterate" is an adjective used as a noun for a group of people, and such a subject takes a plural verb even though it has no plural ending. The clause "since a nineteenth-century archivist discarded the original depositions" names a past starting point for a state that continues, so the present perfect is required. "Has been invisible" has the right tense but treats "The illiterate" as singular. "Were invisible" has the right number but the simple past, which cannot combine with a "since" clause that marks a starting point. "Was invisible" fails on both counts.

SEC26C-03.explanation: The subject of the verb is "the embroidered copes," which is plural; "inventory," "vestment," "feast" and "it" belong to the introductory phrase and its relative clause, not to the main clause. The time phrase "on the eve of the great fire" refers to the single fire that the first sentence reports in the past ("survived the great fire"), so the removal is a completed past event. "Are removed" is plural but follows the present, habitual voice of "which notes ... the feast on which it is worn," which describes routine, not the one past occasion. "Was removed" is past but singular, agreeing with "inventory" or "vestment," and "is removed" fails in both number and tense.

SEC26C-04.explanation: The text before the blank is a complete clause, "the decisive clue had been hiding in plain sight," and the text after it is a second complete clause whose subject, "the ring that all earlier cataloguers had described as plain gold," reaches its verb, "carries," only eleven words later. The second clause explains what the clue was, so a colon joins the clauses correctly. "Sight, the" makes "the ring ..." look like an appositive renaming "the decisive clue," but once "carries" arrives the comma joins two independent clauses, a comma splice. "Sight the" runs the clauses together with no punctuation, a fused sentence. "Sight the," separates "the" from its noun and still fuses the clauses.

SEC26C-05.explanation: The subject is "The copyists," a plural noun; "scriptorium," the singular noun just before the blank, ends the long phrase "at the abbey's small and drafty winter scriptorium." The clause "when floodwaters from the river spread through the lower cloister" names the past moment at which the work was cut off, which is the answer to the historians' question, so the action in progress takes the past progressive. "Have decorated" is plural and suits the lasting result the passage describes, but a present perfect cannot be tied to a specific past moment introduced by "when." "Was decorating" agrees with "scriptorium" rather than "copyists," and "has decorated" fails in both number and aspect.

SEC26C-06.explanation: The subject of the verb is "the editor," a singular noun; "sonnets," just before the blank, is part of the phrase "of the poet's collected sonnets." The object of the revision is the singular "final chapter" (of the "only novel"), which the readers' letters complained about and which contains the digressions "about the hero's childhood"; the sentence's "so ... that" logic links the complaint to the revision, so the pronoun is "it." "Was revising them" has the right verb, but "them" would refer to the sonnets, the letters or the readers, none of which was revised for the novel's second printing. "Were revising it" agrees with "sonnets" rather than "editor," and "were revising them" fails on both counts.

SEC26C-07.explanation: The subject is "its faint final toll," a singular noun phrase, so the verb is singular; "shepherds" and "hills" after the blank are objects of prepositions. The phrase "at the funeral of the bell's first patron" refers to a single occasion: a bell has only one first patron, and that patron's funeral took place in the past, so the statement must be in the past tense. "Is audible" is singular and matches the present-tense description around it ("still hangs," "carries," "keeps"), but it cannot report a single past occasion. "Were audible" is past but plural, agreeing with "shepherds," and "are audible" fails in both number and tense.

SEC26C-08.explanation: The subject is "the restorer," a singular noun; "paintings," just before the blank, ends the phrase "of the hall's six enormous ceiling paintings," and "receipts," which opens the sentence, belongs to the first clause. The clause "before the councillors quit paying for the work" places the cleaning before a completed event in the receipts' past, so the past progressive is required. "Has been cleaning" is singular and suits the lasting damage the sentence describes ("is visibly thinner"), but a present perfect progressive runs up to the present and cannot end before a past event. "Were cleaning" agrees with "paintings," and "have been cleaning" fails on both counts.

SEC26C-09.explanation: The second sentence establishes that the composer left exactly one such volume ("no other record of his working life"), so "his letter book" already identifies it completely. The participial phrase "filled in a cramped hand by the copyist ..." therefore adds information about that one book rather than distinguishing it from other letter books, and a nonrestrictive phrase is set off with a comma. "Book filled" punctuates the phrase as restrictive, which would imply that the composer had several letter books and that scholars used only the one the copyist filled, contradicting the second sentence. "Book; filled" leaves the phrase after the semicolon with no subject or finite verb. "Book filled," separates the participle from its own complement.

SEC26C-10.explanation: The word after the blank, "cast," is the verb of the clause ("cast new letters from melted lead"), so the blank must be a plain noun serving as its subject, not a possessive that would make "cast" a noun. The last sentence says a provincial master "usually trained three or four boys at a time," so the subject is plural: "the apprentices cast new letters." "Apprentices'" and "apprentice's" turn "cast" into a noun ("the apprentices' cast"), leaving the clause without a verb. "Apprentice" forms a grammatical clause on its own, because "cast" has the same form for either number, but it contradicts the several boys each shop trained.

SEC26D-01.explanation: The verb's subject is "a diner," a singular noun, so the verb must be "judges"; "prices" belongs to the opening phrase, and "study" is the object of "in." The thing judged is the "one oddly precise price" named at the start of the sentence, so the pronoun must be the singular "it"; the nearer singular nouns "menu card" and "study" and the later "restaurant" are not what a diner judges "more carefully set." "Judges them" has the right verb, but the only plural it could refer to is the "rounded prices," and the sentence compares the judged item with "the rounded prices," so "them" would compare those prices with themselves. "Judge it" and "judge them" pair a plural verb with the singular subject "a diner."

SEC26D-02.explanation: The subject is "Bilingualism," a singular noun that opens the sentence; "vendors," which follows the blank inside the phrase "among the market vendors," is not the subject. The phrase "at the height of the harbor's grain trade" ties the state to a particular period, and the next sentence says that trade "collapsed," so the period is over and the simple past is required; the present perfect cannot be tied to a finished past period. "Has been widespread" has the right number but the present perfect, which the first sentence's "have argued" and "has shaped" make tempting. "Were widespread" is past but plural, agreeing with "vendors" rather than the subject, and "have been widespread" is wrong in both number and aspect.

SEC26D-03.explanation: The second sentence says the valley had "no other printing press" and that the nearest competing paper came from a city forty miles away, so the town had only one newspaper; "the town's newspaper" already identifies it, and its name, "the Sentinel," is a nonrestrictive appositive that must be set off. With no comma offered, the dash is the correct mark. Leaving the mark out treats "the Sentinel" as a restrictive name that picks one paper out of several, which the second sentence rules out. The semicolon fails because "the Sentinel, whose two reporters attended ..." is a noun phrase with a relative clause, not an independent clause, and placing the comma after "the" splits the article from the name it introduces.

SEC26D-04.explanation: The subject is "Long-term tenants," a plural noun that opens the sentence, so the verb must be plural; "building's" and "increase," which follow the blank, are not the subject. The conditional clause "as long as that increase stays below the ceiling" is in the present tense, so the main verb it conditions must also be present, even though the interrupting "the interviewers found" and the first sentence are in the past. "Were accepting" is plural but past, which clashes with the present "stays." "Is accepting" is present but singular, and "was accepting" is wrong in both number and tense.

SEC26D-05.explanation: The subject is "study," which is singular; the plural possessive "Their" in front of it and the compound "unpaid interns and paid classmates" after it are not the subject. The phrase "since that first recruitment drive" names a past starting point for an activity that continues, and a "since" phrase of this kind requires a perfect form, even though the first sentence narrates the start of the study in the past tense. "Have been following" has the right aspect but a plural verb that agrees with "classmates" or "Their." "Was following" has the right number but the past progressive, which cannot take a "since" phrase marking a starting point. "Were following" fails on both counts.

SEC26D-06.explanation: The subject is "The polite suffix," a singular noun; "verbs," just before the blank, is the object of "on" and is not the subject. "The polite suffix is never under pressure" reads at first as a complete clause, but the clause continues to "disappeared," the past participle of a verb that cannot be made passive or used as an adjective, so it can follow only "has" or "have," never a form of "be." "Have never" chooses the right auxiliary but agrees with "verbs" rather than the subject. "Is never" and "are never" cannot combine with "disappeared," and "are never" is also plural.

SEC26D-07.explanation: The verb's subject is "Field teams," which is plural, so the verb must be "have translated"; "north" and "villages," the nouns just before the blank, belong to the relative clause "that carry ... in the north." The wording being translated is that of "the statistics office's questionnaire," a singular noun named eight words before the blank, so the possessive must be "its"; "north," the nearest singular noun, is not what is translated. "Have translated their" has the right verb but gives the wording to a plural owner: the "hill villages" and the teams wrote no wording, and the provinces' local forms were replaced. "Has translated its" and "has translated their" pair a singular verb with the plural subject "Field teams."

SEC26D-08.explanation: The subject is "the volunteers," a plural noun; "grant," in the opening phrase, and "desk," which ends the adjective phrase "responsible for the branch's homework desk," are singular nouns that are not the subject. The phrase "since the school's closure," sixteen words after the blank and past an interrupting phrase about "former pupils" of a "shuttered" school, marks a past starting point for an activity that continues, so the present perfect is required. "Has coached" has the right aspect but a singular verb that agrees with "desk." "Were coaching" is plural but cannot take a "since" phrase marking a starting point, and "was coaching" fails on both number and aspect.

SEC26D-09.explanation: The words after the blank, "the widow of the shop's first foreman trained in double-entry accounts by her own father," look like a second clause with "trained" as its verb, but "trained ... by her own father" is a passive participle with no helping verb, so the phrase has no main verb: it is a sentence-final appositive describing Ursula Wexler and is set off with a comma. The semicolon would require an independent clause after it, which the phrase is not. The colon would present the phrase as the completion the first clause announces, but that clause already names the bookkeeper in full and announces nothing more; a description added to a name takes a comma. With no mark, the description runs into the name as if it were a title.

SEC26D-10.explanation: The word after the blank, "rules," is the verb of the clause: someone "rules on each procedural objection" before debate resumes. Read as a noun ("the parliamentarian's rules"), it would leave the first clause with no verb, since "resumes" belongs to the "before" clause, so the possessives "parliamentarian's" and "parliamentarians'" fail. The last sentence says the charter assigns that duty to "a lone appointee," so one person rules, and "parliamentarians" is both the wrong number and in disagreement with the singular verb "rules." Only the plain singular "parliamentarian" gives the clause a singular subject for its verb.
